4395.stem:
A university uses gas to heat its buildings. Over a period of 10 weekdays during winter, the gas used each day was measured in megawatts (MW) and the average outside temperature each day was recorded in degrees Celsius ($^\circ$C).

Using $x$ as the average daily outside temperature and $y$ as the total daily gas usage, the equation of the least-squares regression line was found.

The equation of the regression line predicts that when the temperature is $0^\circ$C, the daily gas usage is 236 MW.

The ten temperatures measured were: $0^\circ, 0^\circ, 0^\circ, 2^\circ, 5^\circ, 7^\circ, 8^\circ, 9^\circ, 9^\circ, 10^\circ$.

The total gas usage for the ten weekdays was 1840 MW.

In any bivariate dataset, the least-squares regression line passes through the point $(\bar{x}, \bar{y})$, where $\bar{x}$ is the sample mean of the $x$-values and $\bar{y}$ is the sample mean of the $y$-values.

solution sketch: grid with points (0,236) and (5,184) plotted

parts.latex:
Using the information provided, plot the point $(\bar{x}, \bar{y})$ and the $y$-intercept of the least-squares regression line on the grid.

The mean temperature is the sum divided by 10.
$$\begin{aligned}\bar{x} &= \dfrac{0+0+0+2+5+7+8+9+9+10}{10}\\ &= 5\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\bar{y} &= \dfrac{1840}{10}\\ &= 184\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ (\bar{x},\bar{y}) = (5,184)$$
The $y$-intercept is $(0, 236)$.

parts.latex:
A cricket is an insect. The male cricket produces a chirping sound.

A scientist wants to explore the relationship between the temperature in degrees Celsius and the number of cricket chirps heard in a 15-second time interval.

Once a day for 20 days, the scientist collects data. Based on the 20 data points, the scientist provides the information below.

\begin{itemize}
\item A box-plot of the temperature data is shown.

\exfigure{36_q36_1}
\item The mean temperature in the dataset is $0.525^\circ\text{C}$ below the median temperature in the dataset.
\item A total of 684 chirps was counted when collecting the 20 data points.
\end{itemize}

The scientist fits a least-squares regression line using the data $(x, y)$, where $x$ is the temperature in degrees Celsius and $y$ is the number of chirps heard in a 15-second time interval. The equation of this line is

$$y = -10.6063 + bx,$$

where $b$ is the slope of the regression line.

The least-squares regression line passes through the point $(\bar{x}, \bar{y})$ where $\bar{x}$ is the sample mean of the temperature data and $\bar{y}$ is the sample mean of the chirp data.

Calculate the number of chirps expected in a 15-second interval when the temperature is $19^\circ$ Celsius. Give your answer correct to the nearest whole number.

solutions.latex:
The median temperature is $22$, read from the box-plot, so
$$\bar{x} = 22-0.525 = 21.475$$
$$\bar{y} = \dfrac{684}{20} = 34.2$$
The regression line passes through $(\bar{x},\bar{y})$:
$$\begin{aligned} 34.2 &= -10.6063+b(21.475) \\ b &= \dfrac{44.8063}{21.475} \\ &= 2.08644\ldots \end{aligned}$$
When $x=19$:
$$\begin{aligned} y &= -10.6063+2.08644\ldots\times 19 \\ &= 29.03606\ldots \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ 29 \text{ chirps are expected}$$
criteria: Finds value of $b$, or equivalent merit

Finds the value of $\bar{x}$ and $\bar{y}$, or equivalent merit
Finds the value of $\bar{x}$ or $\bar{y}$ or the median of the temperature, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Correlation: $r=-0.9419$ is close to $-1$, so there is a strong negative linear relationship. Students with more days absent tend to have lower average marks.

Strength: the coefficient of determination is
$$\begin{aligned} r^2 &= (-0.9419)^2 \\ &\approx 0.887 \end{aligned}$$
so about $88.7\%$ of the variation in average mark is explained by the number of days absent. The points on the scatterplot lie close to the line.

Line of best fit $m=96.6-3.84n$:

The gradient $-3.84$ means that, on average, each extra day absent is associated with a drop of about $3.84$ marks.

The intercept $96.6$ is the predicted mark for a student with no absences.

The line can be used for prediction within the data range (about $1.5$ to $11$ days). For example, for 5 days absent:
$$\begin{aligned} m &= 96.6-3.84\times 5 \\ &= 77.4 \end{aligned}$$
Limitations: the line should not be used far outside the range (for instance, a very large $n$ would predict a negative mark). Correlation does not prove that absence causes the lower marks, since other factors may affect both.

Use in discussions: Mr Jensen can show students that missing more days is strongly linked to lower marks, with each day missed costing nearly 4 marks on average, and encourage good attendance.
